title: Irrationality Measure of e
description: The irrationality measure of Euler's number e is exactly 2, the smallest possible value for any irrational number. This follows from the regular continued fraction expansion e = [2; 1, 2, 1, 1, 4, 1, 1, 6, ...].

overview.historicalContext:
**Euler's Discovery and a 241-Year Journey**

In 1737, Leonhard Euler published 'De fractionibus continuis dissertatio,' discovering the remarkable continued fraction expansion e = [2; 1, 2, 1, 1, 4, 1, 1, 6, 1, 1, 8, ...] — a pattern with perfect regularity: the partial quotients cycle as (1, 2k, 1) for k = 1, 2, 3, .... This was the first major structural insight into the arithmetic of e, which Euler had proved irrational 20 years earlier.

The concept of irrationality measure (also called the Liouville-Roth exponent or approximation exponent) emerged from Liouville's 1844 theorem: algebraic numbers of degree d satisfy |α - p/q| > c/q^d, giving μ(algebraic of degree d) ≤ d. Thue (1909), Siegel (1921), and Dyson (1947) progressively improved this until Klaus Roth proved the definitive result in 1955: μ(algebraic irrational) = 2, earning a Fields Medal. Roth's theorem does not apply to transcendental numbers.

For e specifically, C.S. Davis proved in 1978 (Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society) that the linear growth of e's CF partial quotients forces μ(e) = 2. The proof uses the standard CF approximation bounds: |e - p_n/q_n| ≍ 1/(q_n · q_{n+1}), and since q_{n+1}/q_n is bounded (partial quotients grow linearly), this gives |e - p_n/q_n| ≥ c/q_n^2, establishing the upper bound. Combined with Dirichlet's lower bound μ ≥ 2 for all irrationals, this gives μ(e) = 2 exactly.

The contrast with π is stark: despite π's transcendence being proved in 1882 (Lindemann), no CF pattern for π is known, and the best upper bound μ(π) ≤ 7.103 (Salikhov 2008) requires 40+ pages of sophisticated analysis.
overview.problemStatement: **Irrationality measure**: The irrationality measure $\mu(e) = \sup\{\mu : |e - p/q| < q^{-\mu}$ has infinitely many solutions$\}$ equals exactly 2.
overview.text: The irrationality measure of e is exactly 2, proved via the regular continued fraction expansion e = [2; 1, 2, 1, 1, 4, 1, 1, 6, ...].
overview.proofStrategy: Lower bound: Dirichlet's approximation theorem gives $\mu(\alpha) \geq 2$ for all irrationals. Upper bound: The continued fraction of $e$ has partial quotients $a_n = O(n)$, so convergent denominators satisfy $q_{n+1} \leq C \cdot q_n$, giving $|e - p_n/q_n| \geq c/q_n^2$ and hence $\mu(e) \leq 2$.
keyInsights: The irrationality measure μ(e) = 2 follows from a two-part argument: the lower bound μ ≥ 2 for ALL irrationals (Dirichlet), and the upper bound μ ≤ 2 from e's regular CF structure — the two bounds meet exactly

Euler's CF expansion e = [2; 1, 2, 1, 1, 4, 1, 1, 6, ...] is not just elegant; it is why e's approximation quality is precisely quadratic — linear growth of partial quotients forces |e - p_n/q_n| ≥ c/q_n^2

Roth's theorem (1955, Fields Medal) gives μ = 2 for all algebraic irrationals, but e is transcendental so Roth doesn't apply; μ(e) = 2 is a 'coincidence' of CF regularity, not a consequence of general theory

The Mathlib formalization avoids defining μ as a real number; instead it captures μ(e) = 2 as a conjunction: LiouvilleWith 2 e ∧ ∀ p > 2, ¬LiouvilleWith p e — semantically equivalent but more proof-friendly

e is not Liouville (proved from the upper bound axiom), and Irrational e is recovered from LiouvilleWith 2 e via LiouvilleWith.irrational — demonstrating that a single approximation bound subsumes both irrationality and anti-Liouville properties

sections.title: Module Header and Setup
sections.summary: Module docstring defining the irrationality measure and stating the result μ(e) = 2, with references, `maxHeartbeats`/`noncomputable` options, `open Real`, and the `ETranscendentalOQ03` namespace.
sections.mathContext: The irrationality measure $\mu(x) = \sup\{p : \text{LiouvilleWith}(p, x)\}$; the file proves $\mu(e) = 2$.

sections.title: Part I — Irrationality Measure via LiouvilleWith
sections.summary: Connection between irrationality measure and Mathlib's LiouvilleWith: mu(x) = sup{p : LiouvilleWith p x}.
sections.mathContext: The irrationality measure $\mu(x) = \sup\{p \in \mathbb{R} : \text{LiouvilleWith}(p, x)\}$. So $\mu(x) = 2$ iff LiouvilleWith 2 x and $\neg$ LiouvilleWith p x for p > 2.

sections.title: Part II — Lower Bound: mu(e) >= 2
sections.summary: Proves the lower bound: `rat_approx_bounded_den_finite` and `irrational_liouvilleWith_two` give that every irrational has measure ≥ 2 (Dirichlet), and `e_liouvilleWith_two` instantiates this for e.
sections.mathContext: Dirichlet's theorem: for irrational $\alpha$ and $N \geq 1$, $\exists p/q$ with $1 \leq q \leq N$ and $|\alpha - p/q| < 1/(qN) \leq 1/q^2$. This gives infinitely many such approximations, so LiouvilleWith 2 $\alpha$.

sections.title: Part III — Upper Bound: mu(e) <= 2
sections.summary: The upper bound `e_not_liouvilleWith_gt_two` (¬LiouvilleWith p e for p > 2) — the file's sole axiom, justified in the docstring by the continued fraction of e (partial quotients grow linearly, bounding approximation to quadratic).
sections.mathContext: The CF $e = [2; 1, 2k, 1]_{k \geq 1}$ has $a_n = O(n)$, so $q_{n+1} \leq (a_{n+1}+1)q_n$ gives $q_n \leq C^n$. Best approximation: $|e - p_n/q_n| \asymp 1/(q_n q_{n+1})$. Since $q_{n+1}/q_n$ is bounded, $|e - p_n/q_n| \geq c/q_n^2$, giving $\mu(e) \leq 2$. Axiomatized as `e_not_liouvilleWith_gt_two`.

sections.title: Part IV — Main Result: mu(e) = 2
sections.summary: `e_irrationality_measure_eq_two`: combining the lower and upper bounds, the irrationality measure of e is exactly 2.
sections.mathContext: $\mu(e) = 2$ since LiouvilleWith 2 (exp 1) holds (Dirichlet) and $\neg$ LiouvilleWith p (exp 1) for p > 2 (the axiom).

sections.title: Part V — Consequences
sections.summary: `e_not_liouville` (e is not a Liouville number, from the upper bound) and `e_irrational_from_measure` (e is irrational, from the lower bound).
sections.mathContext: Since $\mu(e) = 2 < \infty$, $e$ is not Liouville (Liouville numbers have $\mu = \infty$). From LiouvilleWith 2 e with 2 > 1, irrationality of e follows.

sections.title: Part VI — Context and Comparisons
sections.summary: Docstring comparison of irrationality measures across mathematical constants and discussion of why mu(e) = 2 is remarkable despite being the generic value.

crossReferences.description: Parent proof establishing that e is transcendental. The irrationality measure quantifies the 'quality' of e's transcendence in terms of rational approximation.
Liouville's theorem on rational approximation to algebraic numbers. The LiouvilleWith framework from Mathlib connects both proofs.
Hurwitz's theorem gives the optimal constant sqrt(5) in Dirichlet's approximation, establishing the baseline mu >= 2 for irrationals.

conclusion.summary: The irrationality measure of e is exactly 2, the minimum for any irrational number. This follows from the remarkably regular continued fraction expansion discovered by Euler.
conclusion.implications: Among transcendental numbers, mu = 2 is the 'best behaved' in terms of rational approximation. The fact that mu(e) = 2 while mu(pi) > 2 (likely) reflects the much simpler CF structure of e compared to pi.
openQuestions: Can the continued fraction analysis be fully formalized in Lean 4 via Mathlib's GeneralizedContinuedFraction?
Is mu(e^n) = 2 for all positive integers n?
What is the irrationality measure of e + pi?
